title: Event-Driven API Engineering
stage: Extend the promise across asynchronous time
centralQuestion: How can independent producers and consumers share durable facts without confusing intent, delivery attempts, processing effects, and historical truth?
responsibility: Design, evolve, secure, operate, and verify asynchronous message contracts under delay, duplication, reordering, replay, and consumer failure.
incomingBoundary: The Course 5 API 1.2 service with Security, Reliability, and Performance Profiles 1.0 and migrations 001–009.
outgoingBoundary: Analysis Events API 1.0, Event Profile 1.0, AsyncAPI 3.1.0 contract, CloudEvents 1.0 profile, migrations 010–012, replay and dead-letter policy, and governed consumer declarations.
versionState: HTTP API 1.2 preserved; Analysis Events API 1.0 introduced; AsyncAPI 3.1.0; CloudEvents 1.0-compatible profile; migrations 001–012.
languageStrategy: one primary implementation track plus one comparative reference track

modules.title: Event Thinking, Ownership, and Message Taxonomy
modules.centralQuestion: Which interactions are commands, immutable facts, queries, notifications, or private domain events, and who owns each public fact?
modules.capstoneIncrement: Create the minimal message taxonomy, publication decision record, owner catalogue, and synchronous/asynchronous boundary.
learningOutcomes: separate commands, events, queries, notifications, domain events, and integration events
name events as immutable facts rather than implementation instructions
assign one authoritative producer to every event type
decide whether an asynchronous boundary creates useful temporal or ownership separation
design event granularity without leaking database rows or private implementation models
use subject, correlation, causation, and process identity for distinct purposes
reject event-driven designs that merely replace an ordinary function call with a queue

modules.title: AsyncAPI, CloudEvents, and Contract Architecture
modules.centralQuestion: How do AsyncAPI, CloudEvents, schemas, channels, operations, bindings, and examples form one governed event contract?
modules.capstoneIncrement: Publish Analysis Events API 1.0 with canonical envelopes, message schemas, examples, operation ownership, and deterministic bundles.
learningOutcomes: navigate the AsyncAPI 3.1 document model: servers, channels, operations, messages, components, and bindings
model producer and consumer perspectives without reversing send and receive semantics
apply a constrained CloudEvents 1.0 envelope with course-specific extension attributes
separate envelope validation from payload-schema validation
use JSON Schema identifiers and examples that remain stable after bundling or relocation
distinguish logical channel identity from physical broker address and event type
construct a multi-document contract with offline reference resolution
state exactly what local validation proves and what requires an independent tool or live transport

modules.title: Delivery Semantics, Ordering, Partitioning, and Acknowledgement
modules.centralQuestion: What do acknowledgement, redelivery, ordering, partitioning, lag, and consumer groups actually guarantee?
modules.capstoneIncrement: Implement deterministic delivery attempts, partition order, group independence, acknowledgement expiry, negative acknowledgement, and redelivery.
learningOutcomes: distinguish storage, publication, delivery, processing, effect, and acknowledgement
state at-most-once and at-least-once semantics without hiding loss or duplication
explain why broker-level exactly-once does not automatically create exactly-once business effects
choose a partition key from the smallest domain requiring order
reason about per-partition ordering and cross-partition interleaving
model consumer groups, offsets, in-flight records, acknowledgement deadlines, and redelivery
bound retry and distinguish negative acknowledgement from terminal rejection
measure lag as both record count and age rather than one misleading number

modules.title: Transactional Publication, Inbox Deduplication, and Exactly-Once Effects
modules.centralQuestion: How do producers avoid dual writes and consumers obtain exactly-once effects on top of at-least-once delivery?
modules.capstoneIncrement: Implement transactional outbox publication, inbox deduplication, effect-version identity, and atomic consumer effects.
learningOutcomes: explain the producer dual-write problem and why ordinary exception handling cannot close it
design an outbox row with stable event identity, payload bytes, state, attempts, and leasing
separate broker acceptance from outbox publication completion
make relay retries safe under crash after broker acceptance
design an inbox uniqueness key from event and effect identity
commit inbox state and projection/effect in one local transaction
distinguish one handler invocation, one message delivery, and one committed business effect
extend idempotency across external side effects using a downstream key or another outbox

modules.title: Schema Evolution, Compatibility, Replay, and Historical Truth
modules.centralQuestion: How do event schemas evolve while retained historical events remain immutable and replay remains intelligible?
modules.capstoneIncrement: Classify compatibility, add upcasters, preserve source bytes, define retention, and run bounded dry-run replay.
learningOutcomes: evaluate event-schema changes from producer, current-consumer, and historical-record perspectives
distinguish structural compatibility from semantic compatibility
choose between additive evolution, new major event type, and upcasting
keep immutable historical events separate from corrected projections
design deterministic upcaster chains with explicit source and target versions
plan replay with event bounds, consumer/effect version, checkpoints, and side-effect policy
build new projections alongside old ones and verify before cutover
gate releases on contract validity, compatibility, catalogue completeness, and replay safety

modules.title: Consumer Architecture and Asynchronous Workflows
modules.centralQuestion: How do idempotent consumers, projections, and process managers coordinate asynchronous workflows without hidden synchronous coupling?
modules.capstoneIncrement: Build notification, analytics, audit, and orchestration consumers with stable derived-command identities and explicit state.
learningOutcomes: treat a consumer as a versioned application rather than a handler function
separate projections, external effects, and process coordination
choose orchestration, choreography, or a hybrid from ownership and failure needs
model process-manager transitions idempotently from facts
emit commands without assuming that the requested action succeeded
use correlation and causation to reconstruct asynchronous workflows
handle out-of-order facts without inventing global broker order
define timeouts and compensations as explicit process decisions

modules.title: Event-Time Stream Processing, Windows, Watermarks, and Corrections
modules.centralQuestion: How do event time, processing time, windows, watermarks, lateness, and corrections affect derived results?
modules.capstoneIncrement: Implement windowed analysis metrics, watermark progression, late-event correction revisions, and quarantine.
learningOutcomes: distinguish event time, ingestion time, processing time, and observation time
choose tumbling, sliding, or session windows from the business question
define a watermark as a completeness heuristic rather than a fact that no earlier event exists
handle allowed lateness with revisioned outputs
record beyond-lateness events instead of silently discarding them
deduplicate event-time aggregates by stable event identity
make window state and checkpoints replayable and versioned
explain the difference between operational metrics and business stream projections

modules.title: Event Security, Multi-Tenancy, Privacy, and Trust
modules.centralQuestion: How are producers authenticated, consumers authorized, tenants isolated, payloads minimized, and event bytes protected?
modules.capstoneIncrement: Add producer policy, tenant-scoped subscriptions/replay, exact-byte signatures, freshness, classification, and privacy rules.
learningOutcomes: authenticate producers and consumers independently of message content
authorize publication by producer, source, channel, event type, and tenant
authorize subscriptions by consumer effect and data classification
preserve tenant isolation in subjects, envelopes, partition keys, storage, and projections
minimize sensitive information in long-lived event payloads
sign and verify exact canonical bytes with key identity and freshness policy
distinguish duplicate delivery from hostile message injection or replay
design key rotation and revocation without making retained history unverifiable

modules.title: Event Reliability, Backpressure, Dead Letters, and Recovery
modules.centralQuestion: How do lag, backpressure, retry, poison messages, dead-letter custody, broker failure, and replay storms affect recovery?
modules.capstoneIncrement: Implement failure classification, bounded retry, dead-letter records, lag health, replay controls, and operational runbooks.
learningOutcomes: classify broker, relay, consumer, dependency, schema, security, and capacity failures
apply retry only to transient failures under one budget
bound producer and consumer pressure with admission and backpressure
diagnose lag using count, age, partition distribution, and drain rate
design dead-letter records and repair workflows as controlled operational state
recover from consumer crashes and broker interruption without corrupting effects
prevent replay storms from overwhelming live traffic
reconcile broker progress, inboxes, projections, outboxes, and source truth after incidents

modules.title: Event Platform Governance, Release, and Final Defense
modules.centralQuestion: How are event ownership, compatibility, retention, replay, consumers, evidence, and release decisions governed as a platform capability?
modules.capstoneIncrement: Publish the catalogue, consumer declarations, accepted/rejected release candidates, final defense, and Course 7 handoff.
learningOutcomes: treat the event catalogue as an owned product rather than a topic inventory
define lifecycle stages for draft, active, deprecated, last-published, and retired event versions
gate producer releases on contract, compatibility, catalogue, security, replay, and operational evidence
gate consumer releases on accepted versions, idempotency, lag, dead-letter, replay, and rollback evidence
version partitioning, retention, and schema meaning as public operational commitments
design deprecation and retirement around retained records and consumer migration
produce a minimal sanitized handoff for the next course
defend the complete asynchronous workflow under named failure windows
